en: Cūḷaniddesa:
Exposition of the Pārāyanavagga 17.
Exposition of the Verses Praising the Pārāyana Pathway
This is what the Blessed One said while staying among the Magadhans at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine. Being asked and questioned again and again, he answered the questions of the sixteen brahmin attendants.
"This is what the Blessed One said" means he spoke this *Pārāyana*.
"The Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) is a designation for one who is venerable... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
The Blessed One said this.
"Dwelling among the Magadhans" means dwelling, moving about, acting, protecting, maintaining, and sustaining himself in the country named Magadha.
"At the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya" refers to what is called the Buddha’s seat at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya.
While dwelling among the Magadhans at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, [he spoke] to the sixteen attendant brahmins.
Piṅgiya was a brahmin who was a follower, a foot-servant, an attendant, and a disciple of the brahmin Bāvari.
"Those sixteen by Piṅgiya"—thus it is said.
Thus also regarding the sixteen brahmin attendants.
Or alternatively, those sixteen brahmins were the Buddha, the Blessed One’s foot-followers, personal attendants, and disciples—
thus also regarding the sixteen brahmin attendants.
"Being requested, being asked, he answered the question.
"Requested" (*ajjhiṭṭho*) means requested, entreated.

"Being asked, being asked" (*puṭṭho puṭṭho*) means being asked, being questioned, being entreated, being entreated, being requested, being requested, being inspired with confidence, being inspired with confidence.
"He answered the question" means he answered, declared, taught, laid down, established, opened up, analyzed, clarified, and explained the question.
Thus, being requested and being asked, he answered the question.
Therefore this is said:
“This is what the Blessed One said while dwelling among the Magadhans at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine. Being asked and questioned by the sixteen brahmin attendants, he answered each question.
If one, having understood the meaning and the Dhamma of even a single question, were to practice in accordance with the Dhamma, one would surely go to the further shore of aging and death.
These teachings lead to the further shore.”
Therefore, this discourse on the Dhamma has the designation “Pārāyana.
And even for each individual question—that is, each question of Ajita, each question of Tissa Metteyya, each question of Puṇṇaka, each question of Mettagū, and each question of... [and so forth].
Of the question of Dhotaka, of each of the questions of Upasīva, of each of the questions of Nandaka,
of each of the questions of Hemaka, of each of the questions of Todeyya, of each of the questions of Kappa,
of each of the questions of Jatukaṇṇi, and of each of the questions of Bhadrāvudha.
Whether it be each individual question of Udaya, each individual question of Posāla,
each individual question of Mogharāja, or each individual question of Piṅgiya— that is, each individual question.

"Having understood the meaning and having understood the Dhamma": the question itself is the Dhamma; the answer is the "meaning. Thus, "having understood the meaning" means having known, weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest the meaning.
"Having understood the Dhamma" means having known, weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest the Dhamma.
"Having understood the Dhamma": having understood the meaning, having understood the Dhamma.

"One should practice in accordance with the Dhamma": one should practice the right way of practice, the conformable way of practice, the non-oppositional way of practice, the way of practice that accords with the goal, the way of practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
One should practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

One would indeed go to the further shore of aging and death; for "the further shore of aging and death" is called the Deathless, Nibbāna—that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.

"One would surely go to the further shore of aging and death" means: one would go to the further shore of aging and death, one would reach the further shore, one would touch the further shore, one would realize the further shore—thus, "one would surely go to the further shore of aging and death.
"These phenomena lead to the further shore" means: these phenomena lead to the further shore.

"They cause others to reach the further shore, they lead others to the further shore, they bring others to the very presence of the further shore; they conduce to crossing over aging and death—thus, 'these phenomena lead to the further shore.
Therefore, regarding this discourse on the Dhamma..."
"Therefore" means: for that reason, on that account, by that cause, by that condition, by that source—therefore.
"Of this exposition of the Dhamma" means: of this *Pārāyana*.
Therefore, for this discourse on the Dhamma, "Pārāyana" is indeed its designation.
"Pāra" is said to be the deathless Nibbāna … [as before] … cessation is Nibbāna.
"Ayana" is said to be the path; that is to say:
Right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
"Designation" means: a concept, a common usage, a description, a conventional expression, a name, a naming, a denomination, a linguistic term, a phrasing, a verbal utterance;
thus, "designation" refers specifically to the *Pārāyana*.
Therefore, this is said:
"If one were to understand the meaning and the Dhamma of even a single question and practice in accordance with the Dhamma, one would surely go to the further shore of aging and death.
These teachings lead to the further shore."
"Therefore, this exposition of the Dhamma has the designation 'Pārāyana'.
Thus spoke Ajita, Tissa Metteyya,
Puṇṇaka, and then Mettagū.
Dhotaka and Upasīva,
Nanda and Hemaka,
both Todeyya and Kappa—
And the wise Jatukaṇṇī,
Bhadrāvudha, Udaya,
and the brahmin Posāla as well.
Mogharāja the wise,
and Piṅgiya the great seer—
these approached the Buddha.
Approaching the Buddha, the most excellent one, they questioned the Sage who has perfected his conduct regarding subtle and profound questions.
"These have approached the Buddha.
"These" refers to the sixteen brahmins of the Pārāyanavagga.

"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (*sayambhū*), teacherless (*anācariyaka*), and who has personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena never heard before, having attained omniscience therein and mastery over the powers (*bala*).
In what sense is he "Buddha"?
He is called Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is called Buddha because he awakens the world;

he is called Buddha by virtue of his omniscience, his all-seeing vision, his state of being one who has attained direct knowledge, his state of being one who has reached full expansion, his designation as one whose taints are exhausted, and his designation as one who is undefiled.
He is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from lust; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from hatred; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from delusion;

he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from defilements; he is called "Buddha" because he has traversed the path traveled by only one; he is called "Buddha" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
and he is called "Buddha" because, through the destruction of non-intelligence, he has attained true intelligence.

"Buddha"—this name was not made by his mother, nor made by his father, nor made by his brother, nor made by his sister, nor made by friends and companions, nor made by relatives and kinsmen, nor made by recluses and brahmins, nor made by deities.

This term "Buddha" is a designation realized at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Blessed Buddhas upon the simultaneous acquisition of omniscient knowledge; it is a designation established at the limit of liberation.
"These approached the Buddha" means these approached the Buddha, drew near to him, waited upon him, questioned him, and inquired of him—thus, "these approached the Buddha.
"The Sage with perfected conduct": here, "conduct" refers to the accomplishment of virtue and behavior.

Restraint by virtue is a foot; restraint of the sense faculties is a foot; moderation in eating is a foot; devotion to wakefulness is a foot; the seven true states (*saddhamma*) are feet; and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are feet.
"One perfected in the feet" means one who has perfected the feet, the best feet, the most excellent feet, the foremost feet, the supreme feet, the most sublime feet.

"Seer" (*isi*): the Blessed One is a seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)... [and so on] ...or alternatively, he is a seer because he was sought, searched for, and pursued by beings of great power.
“Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods?
Where is the Bull among Men?”—thus [he spoke] to the seer (isi), the seer perfected in conduct.
"Those who ask ask about the subtle.
Those who ask means those who inquire, entreat, request, and inspire confidence.

"They ask about the subtle" means they ask about that which is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
"Approaching the Best of Buddhas, they asked subtle questions. Regarding "Buddha":
he who is the Blessed One... [as before] ...is the realization-designation (*sacchikā paññatti*), namely, "Buddha."

"Best" means the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the preeminent, the supreme, the sublime Buddha; they approached him, they went to him, they drew near to him, they waited upon him, they questioned him, they inquired of him—it is thus that they "approached the best of Buddhas.
Therefore, this is said:
“They approached the Buddha,
the sage whose conduct is perfected,
asking subtle questions.”
They approached the Best of Buddhas.
To them, the Buddha, being questioned, explained the matter exactly as it is.
With the answering of their questions,
the Sage satisfied the brahmins;
the Buddha gave them his explanation.
"Them" refers to the sixteen brahmins of the *Pārāyanavagga*.
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who... [as above] ...is the realization-designation, namely, "the Buddha.
"He explained" means that the Buddha explained, declared, taught, laid out, established, opened up, analyzed, made plain, and revealed to them.
The Buddha explained them;
"having been asked the question, he answered it exactly as it is.
"Having been asked the question" means having been questioned, requested, entreated, and inspired with confidence.
"Yathātatha" means: he explained in the manner it should be explained; he taught in the manner it should be taught; he described in the manner it should be described;
he established in the manner it should be established; he revealed in the manner it should be revealed;
he analyzed in the manner it should be analyzed; he made clear in the manner it should be made clear.
"He explained it exactly as it should be explained" means that,
when asked a question, he answered it according to reality.
"By the answering of questions" means by the answering of questions through explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and revealing.
"By answering questions,
the Sage satisfied the brahmins.
"Satisfied" means he satisfied, delighted, gladdened, pleased, and made them content.
"Brāhmaṇa" refers to the sixteen Brāhmaṇas of the Pārāyanavagga.
"Muni": "muna" is said to be knowledge ... [and so on] ... "having transcended the net of attachment, he is a muni"—thus the muni satisfied the brāhmaṇas.
Therefore this is said:
"The Buddha, being questioned, explained their question exactly as it was."
By answering their questions,
the Sage satisfied the brahmins.
Satisfied by the One with Vision, they—
They practiced the holy life in the presence of the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who possesses supreme wisdom.
“They were satisfied by the Visionary One”:
“They” refers to the sixteen brahmins of the Pārāyanavagga.
“Satisfied” means they were gratified, thoroughly pleased, inspired with confidence, delighted, and made joyful.
They were satisfied.
"By the One with Vision" means that the Blessed One is possessed of vision by way of five kinds of vision:

he is possessed of vision by the fleshly eye, possessed of vision by the divine eye, possessed of vision by the wisdom-eye, possessed of vision by the Buddha-eye, and possessed of vision by the universal eye.
"How is it that the Blessed One is possessed of vision even by means of the fleshly eye?
... [and so on] ... thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision even by means of the universal eye"—thus they were satisfied by the One Possessed of Vision.
"Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One ... [as described] ... this is the designation based on realization, namely, "Buddha.
"Kinsman of the Sun": the sun is called "Ādicca."
Gotama is by clan, and the Blessed One is also Gotama by clan; the Blessed One is a kinsman and a relative of the sun.
Therefore, the Buddha is called "Kinsman of the Sun"—by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.

"They practiced the holy life" (*brahmacariyam acariṁsu*): "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is said to be the refraining, the abstaining, the complete abstaining, the desisting, the cessation, the non-doing, the non-performance, the non-transgression, the not overstepping the limit, and the destruction of the bridge regarding the attainment of unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*).
Furthermore, in the direct sense, the holy life is called the Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“They practiced the holy life” means they practiced the holy life; they lived having undertaken it, they conducted themselves—it is thus “they practiced the holy life.

“In the presence of the one of supreme wisdom” means in the presence of the one of supreme wisdom, the foremost wisdom, the best wisdom, the most excellent wisdom, the preeminent wisdom, the highest wisdom, the most distinguished wisdom.
"In the presence" means nearby, in the vicinity, close at hand, not far away, in proximity—
to the presence of one of supreme wisdom.
Therefore, this is said:
“Satisfied by the Visionary One,
the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
they practiced the holy life.”
"In the presence of the one of supreme wisdom.
For each and every question,
just as it was taught by the Buddha;
Likewise, whoever should practice thus would go from the hither shore to the further shore.
"Of each question" means: of each question asked by Ajita, of each question asked by Tissa Metteyya... [and so on].
"Of each individual Piṅgiya question" means:
of each individual question.
"Just as it was taught by the Buddha."
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become … [as before] … this is a designation based on realization, namely, "Buddha.
"As taught by the Buddha" means as it was declared, taught, described, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and manifested by the Buddha.
"Whoever would practice accordingly" means:

whoever would practice the right way of practice, the conformable way of practice, the non-opposing way of practice, the way of practice that accords with the goal, and the way of practice in accordance with the Dhamma—
this is "whoever would practice accordingly."
"One should go from the near shore to the far shore": the "far shore" is called the deathless Nibbāna... cessation is Nibbāna;
the "near shore" is called the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.

"One should go from the near shore to the far shore" means: one should go from the near shore to the far shore, one should reach the far shore, one should touch the far shore, one should realize the far shore.
One should go from the near shore to the further shore.
Therefore, this is said:
"For each and every question..."
Just as it has been taught by the Buddha,
so should one practice;
thus one shall go from this shore to the further shore.
One who cultivates the supreme path may go from the hither shore to the further shore;
that path leads to the further shore.
Therefore, it is called "Pārāyana" (The Way to the Further Shore).
"One should go from the hither shore to the further shore": here, the "hither shore" refers to the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations;
the "further shore" refers to the deathless Nibbāna... [and so on].
The destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.

“One would go from the near shore to the far shore” means: one would go from the near shore to the far shore; one would reach the far shore, touch the far shore, and realize the far shore—thus, “one would go from the near shore to the far shore.”
"Cultivating the supreme path": here, the "supreme path" is said to be the Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
"The supreme path" means the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the highest, and the most sublime path.
"Developing" means developing, practicing, and cultivating repeatedly— the supreme path.
"That path is for going to the further shore."
The path, the road, the way, the track,
the direct route, the course, the journey;
the boat and the bridge for crossing.
And every raft is a crossing.
"For the purpose of going to the far shore" means for the purpose of going to the far shore, for reaching the far shore, for arriving at the far shore, for crossing over aging and death—
it is the path for going to the far shore.
"Therefore, 'The Way to the Beyond' (Pārāyana)" means:
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to that cause, that reason, that condition, and that source.
"The beyond" (*pāra*) is called the deathless Nibbāna... [as before] ...cessation is Nibbāna.
“Ayana” is said to mean “path.
“Iti” is the conjunction of words... [and so on] ...this is the sequential order of the words as “iti”;
therefore, it is called “Pārāyana” (The Way to the Further Shore).
Therefore this is said:
"One who develops the supreme path may go from the hither shore to the further shore."
“That is the path for going to the further shore;
therefore, it is called ‘The Way to the Further Shore’ (Pārāyana).
This concludes the seventeenth exposition: the verses in praise of the *Pārāyana*.
